blindSummary:
This country carries elevated danger for trans visitors — it is the most liveable country in its region for trans people, which is a relative statement. Nothing is criminalised; legal gender recognition exists (heavily medicalised: psychiatric boards, and surgery requirements applied in practice); and revealingly, hundreds of trans people fled here from a large neighbouring state after its propaganda law and legal-gender-recognition ban. An international monitoring body recorded 62 anti-LGBTI bias incidents in 2024 — real, but documented and reported, which itself indicates functioning civil-society monitoring groups.

The trajectory is the concern: a petition against open and covert LGBT "propaganda" gained official review by the culture ministry in 2024 (an international human-rights organisation urged rejection), and anti-gender legislators are vocal. Currently there is no propaganda statute, no bathroom law, and no police targeting pattern — police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; risk tracks visibility; the two largest cities are navigable.
blindOutOfScope: Legal-gender-recognition medicalisation and the propaganda petition are resident-facing/trajectory signals.
blindSourceSummaries: A regional LGBTI-rights organisation's annual review 2024 (covering 2023), chapter on this country: hate crimes and police abuse against LGBTQI people continued - an activist nearly run over by a driver who recognised her (no investigation); a trans sex worker harassed, blackmailed and extorted by police posing as clients; hundreds of trans people reportedly came into this country from a large neighbouring state, fleeing that state's war or 'LGBT propaganda' laws; an employment site initially denied an LGBT NGO's registration; anti-LGBTQI statements by politicians, journalists and religious leaders.

International monitoring body's 2024 hate-crime report on this country: no data reported to the body since 2018; no national hate-crime point of contact; civil-society reports for 2024 from local monitoring organisations (including a trans-led group, a women's rights group and others).
An international human-rights organisation (Jul 2024): urges this country to reject an 'LGBT propaganda' bill that would further stigmatise and endanger LGBT people.

A regional LGBT network's report 2024 on violations of the human rights of LGBT people across seven states of this country's wider region (including this one): documented violations of the right to health, barriers faced by LGBT people, and law-enforcement practices, based on monitoring since 2017.

A foreign government's mission to UN bodies (March 2011): post on LGBT rights in the UN context - that government's diplomatic advocacy for SOGI rights at the UN Human Rights Council, relevant to this country's international human-rights environment.

LGBTQ+ news outlet (March 2020): an elite lifestyle magazine made history as the first glossy of the large neighbouring state to feature a trans cover star - a model born in this country to a 'simple but loving family' who believed she was a boy; she identified as a girl from an early age; the neighbouring state's 'gay propaganda' law does not extend to gender identity.

An international human-rights organisation (Sept 2019): a report on this country's supreme court upholding privacy rights - significant in the context of proposed 'propaganda' restrictions targeting LGBT content here.
blindLocalsOnly: The heavily medicalised legal-gender-recognition process (psychiatric boards, surgery requirements) is resident-facing; the propaganda petition and anti-gender legislators are trajectory signals affecting residents.
